question:
Patient note:
A 50-year-old woman, right-hand dominant and employed as an elementary-school art teacher, was sent to the internal-medicine consult service this morning by orthopedics for comprehensive medical clearance prior to a planned elective left total knee arthroplasty to address debilitating tricompartmental osteoarthritis. She ambulated into clinic with a single-point cane, explaining that the cane has become necessary during winter months when her arthritic flares are worst, yet she still supervises recess duty and climbs one flight of stairs to her classroom each day. She reports no episodes of squeezing substernal discomfort, arm or jaw radiation, exertional diaphoresis, or emergency department visits for suspected coronary events; treadmill exercise performed during a wellness challenge at her school six weeks ago allowed her to reach 9 metabolic equivalents without chest pain, palpitations, or abnormal heart rhythm, and a 12-lead electrocardiogram at that time showed normal sinus rhythm with normal intervals and no pathologic Q waves. She likewise denies paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, lower-extremity edema, nocturnal cough, or prior echocardiographic evidence of reduced ejection fraction. Speech has always been fluent, she has never experienced sudden unilateral weakness, vision loss, facial droop, vertigo, or emergent imaging suggestive of acute or chronic cerebral infarction, and her handwriting—critical for her chalk-board sketches—remains steady. With regard to respiratory history, she smoked one pack of cigarettes daily from ages 18 through 38 (20 pack-years) and quit when her first child was born; over the preceding ten years she developed gradually worsening exertional dyspnea and a dry morning cough. Pulmonary function testing obtained last summer demonstrated an FEV1 of 1.8 L, corresponding to 68 % predicted, an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.61 with less than 10 % reversibility after bronchodilator, consistent with fixed airflow obstruction. She currently uses tiotropium 18 µg once every morning, a budesonide–formoterol combination 160/4.5 µg inhaled twice daily, and carries albuterol 90 µg metered-dose inhaler for rescue—typically two puffs twice per week. She has never required hospitalization for respiratory failure, has no home oxygen, and saturates 97 % on ambient air at rest; during stair climbing she notes breathlessness at the second flight but recovers with one-minute pause. In addition, she was diagnosed with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis at age 42 after symmetrical pain and early-morning stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints; baseline hand radiographs then showed small marginal erosions. Current regimen consists of methotrexate 15 mg orally once weekly supplemented by folic acid 1 mg daily, with intermittent celecoxib 200 mg for breakthrough pain. She has never developed nodules, vasculitic rash, scleritis, or interstitial lung disease beyond the airflow limitation described; liver enzyme panels drawn every three months while on methotrexate have remained within normal parameters (AST 24 U/L, ALT 26 U/L, ALP 74 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.4 g/dL, INR 1.0), and abdominal ultrasound last year showed a smooth hepatic contour with no steatosis or portal hypertension. Fasting plasma glucose measured two weeks ago during her annual school-district physical was 96 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c was 5.6 %; she has never been started on metformin or other hypoglycemic drugs, denies polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, neuropathic symptoms, or prior episodes of ketoacidosis, and spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio was 8 mg/g. Serum creatinine this visit is 0.8 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 100 mL/min/1.73 m², blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, and calcium 9.2 mg/dL. She has never experienced hematuria, flank pain, nephrolithiasis, edema, or clinician concern for chronic kidney injury. Past surgical history is limited to an uncomplicated cesarean delivery at age 33; she has no personal history of malignancy, abnormal screening mammography, colonoscopy, or Pap testing, and low-dose chest CT performed two months ago for lung-cancer screening—her tenth anniversary of tobacco cessation—showed upper-lobe centrilobular emphysema but no pulmonary nodules or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. She drinks an occasional glass of red wine on holidays, denies recreational drug use, and her vaccination record is current for influenza and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine. Family history reveals a father with hypertension and a mother with Hashimoto thyroiditis; there is no premature cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease among first-degree relatives. Current medications are methotrexate, folic acid, tiotropium, budesonide–formoterol, albuterol as needed, celecoxib, and over-the-counter vitamin D 1000 IU daily; she has no medication allergies. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, chills, weight loss, night sweats, dyspepsia, melena, hematochezia, jaundice, photosensitive rash, Raynaud phenomenon, hemoptysis, dizziness, syncope, or cognitive lapse. On examination she appears well, speaks in full sentences, and is oriented to person, place, and time. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg seated in the left arm, heart rate 74 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97 % on room air, weight 75 kg, height 167 cm, body-mass index 27 kg/m². Conjunctiva are pink, sclerae anicteric. Carotid pulses are brisk without bruit, jugular venous pulsation is less than 3 cm above the sternal angle, and the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced. Cardiac auscultation reveals normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung fields are hyperresonant with diminished breath sounds bilaterally and scattered end-expiratory wheezes but no crackles. Abdomen is soft, non-tender, with normal bowel sounds and no organomegaly. Hands show mild fusiform swelling of the second and third MCPs bilaterally, ulnar deviation absent, grip strength 4/5, and full passive range of motion; there are no tophi or Heberden nodes. Distal pulses are 2+ and symmetric in radial, femoral, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries; capillary refill is under two seconds and there is no ankle edema or trophic skin change. Neurologic screening demonstrates intact cranial nerves, normal strength in all major muscle groups, symmetric reflexes, and heel-to-toe gait limited by knee pain rather than weakness. Skin examination reveals no lesions, ulcers, or nailfold capillary abnormalities. A repeat post-bronchodilator spirometry performed in clinic confirms FEV1 1.8 L (67 % predicted) and FEV1/FVC 0.60, unchanged from prior baseline. Chest radiograph today shows hyperinflated lung volumes with flattened diaphragms and clear parenchyma. Electrocardiogram in clinic demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 72 beats/min with normal axis and intervals, no ST-T segment deviation. She seeks counsel on perioperative pulmonary management, potential methotrexate withholding around surgery, and strategies to expedite postoperative rehabilitation while minimizing flare of her joint disease and preserving current respiratory stability.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums an age score and weighted points for qualifying chronic diseases present at assessment.
- Age 50: the 50–59 age band = 1.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: emphysema with persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction (FEV₁/FVC 0.60) = 1.
- Rheumatic disease: established seropositive rheumatoid arthritis = 1. Knee osteoarthritis does not add a separate point.
- Other CCI conditions: none documented = 0.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 3.
Final answer: 3
